sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark.

questions.q: State 'True' or 'False' about the sound effects used in radio formats: (i) Sound does not play any role in evoking interest. (ii) Sound can be used to enhance certain moods.
Radio documentaries are based on ______ and ______ events.
Match the radio formats with their duration: (a) Radio talk (b) Radio discussion with (i) 10–15 minutes (ii) 15–30 minutes.
Fill in the blanks: A phone-in programme is also called ______ programming; AIR started its internet services on ______.
Match: (i) Announcements (ii) Commentary (iii) Interview (iv) Discussion (v) Radio talk with (a) Republic Day parade (b) oldest radio format (c) inform listeners (d) asking questions (e) moderator.
State true or false: (i) Phone-in programmes need advance publicity. (ii) Radio on internet needs a frequency licence.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: List any four factors taken into account for making a radio talk show.
questions.answer: Audience profile (literacy, language), topic, duration, expert speakers, timing, simple scripted spoken style.

questions.q: Discuss any two ingredients of the radio programme formats.
questions.answer: Spoken word (human voice, scripted) and music; also sound effects which evoke interest, comedy or moods.

questions.q: What is a vox pop?
questions.answer: A Latin phrase meaning 'voice of people': one or two questions are put to ordinary people to measure public opinion on a current topic.

questions.q: What is a signature tune?
questions.answer: A piece of music specific to a programme, like the masthead of a magazine, played at the beginning.

questions.q: What is a radio bridge?
questions.answer: Connecting different radio stations across the country so that people at different places can interact.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Briefly describe any three types of radio programmes that fall under the 'spoken word' format.
questions.answer: Radio talk: an expert speaks on a topic; radio interview: questions put to a person; radio discussion: experts and a moderator discuss a public issue (also news, drama and commentary).

questions.q: Explain any three spoken-word radio formats with examples.
questions.answer: Radio talk (a 10–15 minute talk), radio discussion (a moderated panel on a social issue) and running commentary (cricket or Republic Day parade).

questions.q: Discuss three information technology based radio formats, providing examples.
questions.answer: Phone-in programme (listeners' live queries to experts), radio bridge (connecting stations during elections) and radio on internet (AIR, BBC online).

questions.q: Define radio documentaries and radio dramas with examples.
questions.answer: A radio documentary uses real sounds, people and facts creatively (a feature on a village); a radio drama is a play using only voice, music and sound effects (a wedding scene using shehnai).

sections.title: Long answer question. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Explain with examples the different formats of radio programmes.
questions.answer: Announcements, talk, interviews, discussions, documentaries, drama, commentaries, magazine programmes, news and music, plus IT-based formats such as phone-in, radio bridge and internet radio.

questions.q: Discuss the factors to be taken into account before making a radio programme.
questions.answer: Audience facts such as population, literacy, language, occupation, health, climate, power supply and income decide the language, type and timing of programmes.
